prompt_text: Roleplay  a peasant from 12th century England. Explain how you feel about books
response_text:
I am a simple farmer, born in the year of our Lord twelve‑hundred‑seventy‑two, and I have never learned to read the letters that the monks and the clerks of the great churches write upon parchment. Yet, even in my humble cottage, the word “book” has a weight to it that is as heavy as the iron of a ploughshare.

When I first saw a book, it was in the great hall of the parish church, a place where the whole village would gather to hear the priest speak of the Lord’s will. The book lay upon a wooden stand, its cover of leather, its pages of white‑tanned skin. The monks, with their long white hair and their robes of coarse wool, would sit upon the benches and read aloud from it. The sound of their voices, the turning of the pages, the faint scent of ink and parchment—those were the things that made my heart stir.

I have never had a book in my own hands. The only books I have ever known are those that the priest reads to us, the Gospels, the Psalms, the Book of Common Prayer. They are the only books that touch my life. To me, a book is a holy thing, a vessel of God’s word. It is a thing that the Church keeps in its vaults, guarded by men who have spent their lives learning to read. It is a thing that is not for the common folk, but for the clergy and the nobles who can afford the cost of parchment and the labor of the scribes.

I have heard the tales of the monks who travel from one abbey to another, copying the same book over and over, each time adding a new line, a new illustration. They say that the book is a treasure, a record of the past, a guide for the future. I have also heard the stories of the great libraries in the cities, where scholars sit for hours upon hours, reading and debating. Those are places that are far beyond my reach.

So, how do I feel about books? I feel a mixture of awe and humility. Awe, because the book is a thing that contains the words of God, the laws of the land, the stories of saints and kings. Humility, because I am a peasant, and I have no means to read or to own a book. I am content to listen to the priest read the words aloud, to hear the stories of the saints, to feel the presence of the divine in the words that are spoken. I do not know the words that are written, but I know that they are holy, that they are a gift from God, and that they are a source of comfort and guidance.

In my heart, I wish that one day I could hold a book in my hands, feel the weight of its pages, and read the words that the monks have written. Until then, I will continue to listen, to learn, and to pray, trusting that the words of the book will guide me through the hardships of the harvest and the trials of life.
